title: The Extractor Arm Quiz
intro: Heads up: this one is all about reading code carefully. To unlock the Extractor code you need a PERFECT score, 10 out of 10. Most people need a few tries, and that's normal.

questions.q: What is an enum?
questions.correct: A fixed list of named choices
wrong: A number between 0.0 and 1.0
A method that runs every single loop
A list that can keep growing forever
questions.explain: An enum lists every choice by name, like STOWED and DEPLOYED. A variable of that type can only hold one of those names.

questions.q: enum State { STOWED, DEPLOYED }  What can a State variable hold?
questions.correct: Only STOWED or DEPLOYED
wrong: Any number from 0.0 to 1.0
Any word the programmer types
STOWED, DEPLOYED or OFF
questions.explain: An enum is a closed list. Only the names inside the braces are allowed, so there are no typos and no mystery values.

questions.q: Why use an enum instead of a boolean like deployed?
questions.correct: It reads like English and is easy to extend
wrong: Booleans aren't allowed anywhere in Java subsystems
Enums make the servo move a lot faster
A boolean would need two servos to work
questions.explain: A boolean works for two positions, but State.DEPLOYED is clearer, prints its name on telemetry, and a third position is just one more word.

questions.q: Why is the enum State declared public?
questions.correct: So the TeleOp can name it to show it on telemetry
wrong: So any class can move the servo directly
Because every enum in Java has to be public
So the servo can read its own position back
questions.explain: Being able to name the type (Extractor.State) is different from being able to change the arm. The state field itself stays private.

questions.q: private static final double STOWED_POS = 0.10;  What does final mean here?
questions.correct: The value never changes while the program runs
wrong: It's the last line in the class
Only the TeleOp can read the value
The arm moves there at the very end of the match
questions.explain: final means once it's set, it can't be changed. That's what makes it a constant.

questions.q: Why write STOWED_POS instead of typing 0.10 everywhere?
questions.correct: One line to retune, and the code explains itself
wrong: Java can't use plain numbers inside methods
Named constants make the servo a little bit stronger
Typing 0.10 makes the arm move the wrong way
questions.explain: Change STOWED_POS once and every place that uses it updates. And the name tells the reader what the number means.

questions.q: What is a magic number?
questions.correct: A bare number in code with no name explaining it
wrong: A number that changes itself every single loop
The servo position that unlocks the reward
A number bigger than 1.0 that servos ignore
questions.explain: 0.75 alone doesn't say why it's 0.75. DEPLOYED_POS does. Naming numbers keeps code readable.

questions.q: public void deploy() { state = State.DEPLOYED; }  What does calling deploy() do?
questions.correct: Sets state to DEPLOYED; update() moves the servo
wrong: Moves the servo right away and waits for it
Lowers the arm, waits two seconds, raises it
Reads where the servo is pointing right now
questions.explain: Commands only change the field. The next update() turns the new state into a servo position, the same pattern as every subsystem.

questions.q: Which method actually sends a number to the servo during the match?
questions.correct: update()
wrong: deploy()
getState()
isDeployed()
questions.explain: deploy() and stow() only change the state. update() is the one place that calls servo.setPosition(...) every loop.

questions.q: Who calls the Extractor's update() every loop?
questions.correct: The scheduler, through robot.update()
wrong: The driver, by pressing D-pad down
The servo itself, after it finishes moving
The constructor, once during INIT
questions.explain: Robot keeps a list of subsystems and robot.update() calls each one's update(), every loop.

questions.q: switch (state) { case STOWED: servo.setPosition(STOWED_POS); break; case DEPLOYED: servo.setPosition(DEPLOYED_POS); break; }  If state is DEPLOYED, which number is sent?
questions.correct: DEPLOYED_POS
wrong: STOWED_POS
Both, one after the other
Nothing; the switch is skipped
questions.explain: The switch jumps to the case that matches the state, here DEPLOYED, and runs it until the break.

questions.q: What does break do at the end of a switch case?
questions.correct: Leaves the switch so the next case doesn't run
wrong: Stops the whole OpMode right away and resets it
Disconnects the servo for safety
Pauses the robot for one loop
questions.explain: break means 'this case is done, leave the switch.' Without it, Java keeps going into the next case.

questions.q: You forget the break after case STOWED. The state is STOWED. What happens?
questions.correct: It falls through and runs the DEPLOYED case too
wrong: Java skips the STOWED case completely and moves on
The arm stops moving forever after
Nothing at all changes in how it runs
questions.explain: Without break, Java 'falls through' into the next case. The servo gets DEPLOYED_POS last, so the arm would go down. A sneaky bug!

questions.q: public boolean isDeployed() { return state == State.DEPLOYED; }  The arm is stowed. What does it return?
questions.correct: false
wrong: true
STOWED
questions.explain: == compares. Is STOWED equal to DEPLOYED? No, so the answer is false.

questions.q: What's the difference between = and == in Java?
questions.correct: = stores a value; == compares two values
wrong: = is for numbers; == is for words
They mean exactly the same thing
== stores the value twice, just to be extra safe
questions.explain: state = State.DEPLOYED puts a value in. state == State.DEPLOYED asks a yes/no question.

questions.q: if (gamepad1.dpad_down) robot.extractor.deploy();  The driver holds D-pad down for 30 loops. What happens?
questions.correct: deploy() runs 30 times, and the arm just stays down
wrong: The arm flips down and up 30 times
The arm lowers a little farther each time, 30 times
Nothing, because it needs edge detection
questions.explain: Setting the state to DEPLOYED again and again changes nothing after the first time. The arm is already down.

questions.q: Why doesn't the extractor need edge detection like the intake's A button?
questions.correct: Each button always means the same thing
wrong: D-pad buttons only work once per match
Servos ignore repeated commands on their own
Edge detection only works with motors
questions.explain: Edge detection matters when a button FLIPS something. Here down always means deploy and up always means stow, so repeats don't matter.

questions.q: Why use two buttons (down and up) instead of one toggle button?
questions.correct: The driver never has to remember the arm's state
wrong: The gamepad only has two buttons left
Toggle buttons aren't allowed by the FTC game rules
One button would need a second servo
questions.explain: With a toggle, the driver must remember if the arm is up or down. With two buttons, up is always up.

questions.q: A team wants LB to toggle the arm instead. What do they need to add?
questions.correct: Edge detection, so one press flips it once
wrong: A second servo to move it in the other direction
A timer that waits two seconds
Nothing; toggles work on their own
questions.explain: A toggle flips. Without edge detection, holding LB for 20 loops would flip it 20 times. Compare with previousLB, like the intake's A button.

questions.q: Which D-pad button lowers (deploys) the arm?
questions.correct: D-pad down
wrong: D-pad up
D-pad left
D-pad right
questions.explain: Down lowers it and up raises it, so the button matches the motion.

questions.q: In the simulator, which keyboard key acts as D-pad down?
questions.explain: ; is D-pad up and / is D-pad down. (, and . are D-pad left and right.)

questions.q: What does the arm do the moment INIT is pressed?
questions.correct: It moves to the stowed position right away
wrong: Nothing at all until the driver presses START
It lowers to show that it's working
It slowly searches for its position
questions.explain: The constructor runs at INIT and calls servo.setPosition(STOWED_POS). A positional servo jumps there immediately, so keep hands clear.

questions.q: What does the try/catch in the Extractor constructor do?
questions.correct: If there's no extractor servo, store null instead of crashing
wrong: Tries to move the arm twice in case it gets stuck
Catches the arm if it falls down too fast
Checks the battery before the servo moves
questions.explain: hardwareMap.get throws an error if the device isn't configured. catch grabs that error so the rest of the robot keeps running.

questions.q: Why does update() begin with if (servo == null) return; ?
questions.correct: On a robot without an extractor, skip the servo
wrong: To make the servo move faster each loop
Because update() must always return a number to Robot
To stop the robot whenever the arm is down
questions.explain: If the servo wasn't found, it's null, and calling setPosition on null would crash. Returning early skips it safely.

questions.q: What does return; do inside update()?
questions.correct: Leaves the method right away
wrong: Sends the servo back to stowed
Starts the method again from the top
Returns the arm into the robot
questions.explain: return ends the method. Nothing below it runs this time.

questions.q: On your robot, D-pad down raises the arm instead of lowering it. What's one fix?
questions.correct: Add setDirection(REVERSE), or swap the two numbers
wrong: Press D-pad down twice as fast
Plug the servo into a motor port
Delete the enum and use a boolean instead of it
questions.explain: Either reverse the servo in the constructor or swap STOWED_POS and DEPLOYED_POS. Both make 'down' go down.

questions.q: What is the Extractor Calibrate OpMode for?
questions.correct: Finding the servo numbers for up and down
wrong: Driving the robot during a real match
Testing the battery before each match
Making the arm move by itself on a timer
questions.explain: You move the arm with the stick, read its number on telemetry, and write the up and down numbers into the constants.

questions.q: position -= gamepad1.right_stick_y * 0.003;  Pushing the stick all the way up makes right_stick_y = −1. What happens to position?
questions.correct: It gets bigger by 0.003 each loop
wrong: It gets smaller by 0.003 each loop
It jumps straight to 1.0
It stays exactly the same
questions.explain: −1 × 0.003 = −0.003, and subtracting a negative adds: position goes up by 0.003 every loop.

questions.q: position = Math.max(0.0, Math.min(1.0, position));  If position is 1.2, what is it after this line?
questions.explain: Inside first: Math.min(1.0, 1.2) is 1.0. Then Math.max(0.0, 1.0) is 1.0. The line keeps position between 0 and 1.

questions.q: position = Math.max(0.0, Math.min(1.0, position));  If position is −0.05, what is it after this line?
questions.explain: Math.min(1.0, −0.05) is −0.05. Then Math.max(0.0, −0.05) is 0.0. Too low gets pulled up to 0.

questions.q: When does the Extractor's constructor run?
questions.correct: Once, when Robot builds it with new
wrong: Every loop, right before update()
Every time D-pad down is pressed
Only when the arm is deployed
questions.explain: new Extractor(hardwareMap) runs the constructor once, during INIT, to set the object up.

questions.q: Where does the line public final Extractor extractor; go?
questions.correct: Robot.java, with the other subsystem fields
wrong: Extractor.java, just above the State enum list
MecanumDrive.java, inside the loop
ExtractorCalibrate.java, at the top
questions.explain: Robot holds one field per subsystem so the rest of the code can say robot.extractor.

questions.q: Why does Robot's constructor call subsystems.add(extractor)?
questions.correct: So the scheduler calls its update() every loop
wrong: So the servo gets more power from the hub
So the arm starts in the deployed position
So the TeleOp can delete it later on
questions.explain: robot.update() loops through the subsystems list. If the extractor isn't on it, its update() never runs and the servo never moves.

questions.q: Why is the servo field declared private?
questions.correct: Only Extractor's own code should move it
wrong: Private servos move more smoothly
So the TeleOp can move it directly
Because servos can't be public in Java
questions.explain: Keeping the servo private means every move goes through deploy()/stow() and update(), so nothing can confuse the arm behind its back.

questions.q: telemetry.addData("Extractor", robot.extractor.getState());  The arm is deployed. What shows on the Driver Hub?
questions.correct: Extractor: DEPLOYED
wrong: Extractor: true
Extractor: 0.75
Extractor: 1
questions.explain: getState() gives back the enum value, and telemetry prints an enum by its name. That's one reason enums beat booleans.

questions.q: How is the extractor different from the old dumper?
questions.correct: The driver decides when, with no timers
wrong: The extractor runs a timed routine by itself
The dumper had no servo, the extractor has one
The extractor needs a stopwatch to work
questions.explain: The dumper ran raise, hold, lower on timers after one press. The extractor just goes where the driver says, when the driver says.

questions.q: When would a timed sequence, like the old dumper's, be the better choice?
questions.correct: When one press should run a whole routine
wrong: When the driver wants control of every step
When the mechanism has only two positions
When the robot has no servos at all
questions.explain: Timers shine when a mechanism should do several steps on its own. When the driver should decide, simple commands are better.

questions.q: A team adds HALFWAY to the enum. What else must they change in update()?
questions.correct: Add a case HALFWAY with its own servo number
wrong: Nothing; the switch handles it automatically
Delete the STOWED case to make room for it
Swap the servo for a continuous-rotation one
questions.explain: The switch only knows the cases you write. HALFWAY needs its own case, its own constant (like HALFWAY_POS) and a command to choose it.

questions.q: public State getState() { return state; }  What does getState() do?
questions.correct: Gives back the current state without changing it
wrong: Moves the arm to a brand new state and holds it
Resets the arm back to stowed
Asks the servo where it really is
questions.explain: A getter just reports. Other code can look at the state, but only deploy() and stow() can change it.

questions.q: The arm is STOWED. In one loop the driver holds BOTH D-pad down and up. The code runs: if (dpad_down) deploy(); then if (dpad_up) stow();  What is the state after that loop?
questions.correct: STOWED, because stow() ran last
wrong: DEPLOYED, because deploy() ran first
Both at once, so it stops halfway
The program crashes with an error
questions.explain: Lines run in order. deploy() sets DEPLOYED, then stow() sets STOWED. The last one wins.

questions.q: Servo positions in FTC code are numbers between...
wrong: 0 and 360
0 and 100
questions.explain: setPosition takes 0.0 to 1.0. What angle that means depends on the servo and how it's mounted.

questions.q: Why must the servo be named exactly extractor in the robot configuration?
questions.correct: The code looks it up by that exact name
wrong: Servos only work with lowercase names
FTC rules require every servo be named
The name decides which way it turns
questions.explain: hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "extractor") searches the configuration for that name. A different name means 'not found'.
